$doc: Generated by evals/run.mjs alongside evals/results.json and the <!-- content:evals-* --> regions of evals.html. Do not edit; `node evals/run.mjs --check` byte-compares this file and names it when it is stale.

This is a serialization of the SAME numbers those two artefacts carry, structured so a renderer does not have to parse HTML or re-derive anything. Every figure was computed once, by the run that wrote all three.

EVERY STRING UNDER `regions` IS HTML, already escaped exactly as it appears in evals.html. Render it as markup (dangerouslySetInnerHTML or equivalent), not as plain text, or an entity such as `<` in the paired-test note will render literally. Do not escape it again.

`regions[name].html` is the exact line array written between that region's markers in evals.html, for byte-verification. evals.html indents each line to its marker's column; these lines carry only their own relative indent. Prefer the structured fields beside it for rendering — `html` exists so a second renderer can prove it is showing the same thing.

`regions['evals-reading']` is PROSE, authored in content/evals.json by the repo owner and substituted here. It has no structure to recover: ship each paragraph verbatim. Never re-word it, never re-flow a sentence around a number.

n is small and the intervals are wide. Read `summary.confidence`, `summary.questions` and the per-metric `half` strings out of this file — never hard-code a sample size or a half-width into a page or a document, because both have moved before.
A skipped arm is `regions['evals-table'].skipped` and a shorter `arms` array. It is never a substituted number from elsewhere; render the skip.

pairedNote: Exact two-sided McNemar on hit@3, paired question by question. Only discordant questions —
ones the two arms disagree about — carry information, so the counts are small even where the
margin is large. Five discordant pairs cannot reach p<0.05 under an exact test; 0.0625 is
the floor. A significant result here is a real difference; a non-significant one is a
difference this question set is too small to detect, not a demonstration of equality.
separabilityNote: separability is the fraction of (answerable, unanswerable) pairs that any top-1 score cut
orders correctly, ties counted half. It was previously printed beside abstain as independent
corroboration and it is not: for an arm that refuses, most pairs are won by the refusal rather
than by the score, which is why two arms with completely different score scales reported the
same figure. Only the last chip on each row is about ranking.

paragraphs: Plain lexical search won on ranking, and the structured arm lost. BM25 reaches 67.3% hit@3 and 0.581 MRR; navigating by name reaches 46.9% and 0.484. The design being evaluated here expected the opposite, and the number is reported the way it came out. The reason is visible in the failures: a name match fires on whichever entity happens to share a word with the question, and on questions phrased the way people actually phrase them — “what user research methods does he use?” — no entity is named at all. The corpus is small, single-author and lexically consistent, which is precisely the condition under which BM25 is strong.

Knowing when to say nothing is where they separate, and it is not close. BM25 abstains on 6 of 16 unanswerable questions. It returns a confident ranked list for “did he ever work at Google?” — the word appears eight times in the corpus, in Google Analytics, Google Play and Google AI Studio, none of them an employer — and for “what are his salary expectations?”, and for “does he speak Japanese?”. The tools arm abstains on 13 of 16, because no entity was named. That is not a tuning artefact; it is the difference between matching words and resolving identifiers.

Fusing the two rankings made both worse. Tools-first with BM25 appended scores 51.0% hit@3 — below BM25 alone — and abstains on nothing, because the fallback always fires. It inherits the weaker ranking and the weaker judgement. That result killed the originally proposed shape, which is the most useful thing this table did.

What the failure suggested instead. Stop fusing rankings and split responsibilities: let the name match decide whether the corpus covers the question, and let BM25 decide what comes back once it does. That arm — tools-gated — holds 22.4% hit@3 and 0.679 separability, tied for best in the table, while raising the abstention rate to 93.8%. Roughly seven points of ranking traded for the entire ability to say “not on file”. It is labelled post-hoc everywhere it appears, because it was written after seeing the first three arms on this same question set; it is a hypothesis this run suggests, not a result this run establishes, and it needs questions written after it to become one.

Two holes in the corpus, found by the eval rather than by a reviewer. Location, availability and contact details live in content.json as structured fields and appear in no chunk, so “where is he based?” cannot be answered by any search over prose — the only chunk containing the word “Sofia” is the education line, about Sofia University, and BM25 duly returns something else entirely. Separately, the 2007–2009 quality assurance role has no bullet points, so the content build produced no chunk for it at all: the role is in the index and invisible to search, and every arm scores zero on it. Both are why the tool layer reads structured fields directly instead of searching for them.

One question no arm could answer, and it is the case for embeddings. “How far has he run?” shares no term with “42 km. Marathon finisher.” — lexical search returns nothing at all. That is the exact shape of question a semantic retriever exists for. The embeddings arm has since been run: it answers this question and wins every retrieval class, at 81.6% hit@3 against BM25's 67.3%. The argument became a measurement.

The point the corpus statistics make on their own. The complete table of contents — every project id, title, client, tag and one-line summary, every role and span — is a few thousand characters. It fits in the system prompt. A retriever exists to solve “I cannot enumerate what is in here”; when the whole index fits in the prompt, that problem does not exist, and provisioning a stateful, billed service to solve it anyway is a decision about a résumé rather than about a corpus. That argument survives this table. The claim that structured lookup also ranks better did not.
